p.seg: "Xú Zhì 徐穉, courtesy name Rúzǐ 孺子,
was a native of Nánchāng 南昌 in Yùzhāng 豫章.
He possessed a refined and outstanding
demeanor,
surpassing the world and detached from common customs.
He was repeatedly recommended by various high officials,
though he never accepted office.
When he died,
people traveled thousands of miles to attend his funeral.
He would always prepare a roasted chicken,
soak cotton in wine,
dry it in the sun,
and use it to wrap the chicken.
He would go directly to the outside of the tomb tunnel he was attending,
soak the cotton in water,
offer a dòu 斗 (unit of dry measure) of cooked rice,
use white reeds as a mat,
and place the chicken in front.
After libating the wine,
he would pay his respects and leave immediately,
never seeing the bereaved family."
The chief clerk reported,
"The general sentiment is that the Prefect should enter the office first."
Chén 陳 said,
"King Wǔ 武 bowed to the gate of Shāng Róng 商容,
not even taking time to warm his mat.
Xǔ Shūchòng 許叔重 said,
'Shāng Róng 商容
The worthy man of Yin,
was the teacher of Laozi."
Kneeling in the carriage, he made a gesture of respect.
"My showing respect to the worthy,
Yuán Hóng's *Annals of the Hàn* says:
what is unacceptable about that!"
"Fān, while in Yùzhāng,
specially prepared a couch solely for Zhì,
and when he left, it was hung up,
showing such respect."
Zhōu Zǐjū often said:
"If I do not see Huáng Shūdù for a month,
then feelings of narrowness and stinginess will be reborn in me."
Zǐjū saw him separately.
The *Diǎn Lüè* says:
"Huáng Xiàn, styled Shūdù,
was a man from Shènyáng in Rǔnán.
Contemporary commentators all said
'Yán Zǐ has been reborn'.
But his clan came from a humble and rustic background,
and his father was a cattle doctor.
Xún Jìhé of Yǐngchuān held Xiàn's hand and said:
'You are my model.'
Later, seeing Yuán Fènggāo, he said:
'Your state has a Yán Zǐ,
how can you not know him?'
Fènggāo said:
'Have you seen my Shūdù?'
Dài Liáng, when young, was accustomed to being subordinate.
When he saw Xiàn, he would humble himself even further,
feeling disappointed as if he had lost something.
His mother asked,
"Why are you unhappy?
Did you revert to acting like someone you learned from a veterinarian?"
Liáng said,
"Looking at him, he seemed to be ahead,
but suddenly, he was behind.
He is what I would call a good teacher."
Guō Línzōng arrived at Rǔnán
to visit Yuán Fènggāo.
*The Later Hàn Book* says:
"Guō Tài, styled Línzōng,
was from Jièxiū in Tàiyuán.
Tài was orphaned young.
At the age of twenty,
he traveled to study, arriving at Chénggāo,
at the secluded residence of Qū Bóyàn.
Lacking food,
and with clothes that barely covered his body,
he lived frugally and savored the principles (of life),
not changing his cheerful demeanor.
Lǐ Yuánlǐ, upon seeing him once, praised him, saying,
'I have seen many scholars,
but none are like Línzōng.'
After his death,
Cài Bójīe wrote a stele inscription for him,
He said:
"When I write epitaphs for others,
I have never been without a feeling of shame,
only when writing the 'Bēi Sòng for Guō Yǒudào' am I without shame."
Initially,
he was recommended as a virtuous gentleman.
Tài said:
"Observing the celestial phenomena and human affairs,
what Heaven has abandoned cannot be supported."
Thereupon, he declined, claiming illness."
The *Rǔnán Xiānxián Zhuàn* says:
"Yuán Hóng, courtesy name Fènggāo,
was from Shènyáng.
He befriended Huáng Shūdù in his childhood,
and recommended Chén Zhòngjǔ from his village lane.
(He) died."
Having been summoned as a clerk by the Grand Commandant,
his carriage did not stop on its track,
nor did the bells cease their ringing.
When visiting Huáng Shūdù,
he would stay for days and nights.
People asked the reason for this?
Lín Zōng said:
"Shūdù is vast
like a ten-thousand-*qǐng* pond.
Settle it, and it won't clear;
disturb it, and it won't cloud.
His capacity is deep and broad,
"difficult to measure."
The *Tài Bié Zhuàn* says:
"Xuē Gōngzǔ asked him,
Tài said:
'The vessels of Fènggāo
are like a flood;
though clear, they are easily filled.'"
Lǐ Yuánlǐ's style and character were outstanding and refined;
he held himself to high standards,
desiring to make the distinction between right and wrong in the world of morality his own responsibility.
Xuē Yíng's *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
"Lǐ Yīng, styled Yuánlǐ,
was a native of Xiāngchéng in Yǐngchuān.
He possessed lofty aspirations and clear understanding,
and had both literary and martial talents.
He was promoted to Director of the Capital Region (Sīlì Xiàowèi)
and committed suicide because of the partisan affairs."
Later scholars,
those who were able to enter his hall,
all considered it as ascending the Dragon Gate.
[Liú's commentary]: *Sān Qín Jì* says:
"The Dragon Gate,
also called Héjīn,
is nine hundred *lǐ* away from Cháng'ān.
The water is suspended and cut off;
turtles and fish cannot ascend it;
those that do ascend will transform into dragons."
Lǐ Yuánlǐ once praised Xún Shū and Zhōng Hào.
The *Records of Former Worthies* states:
"Xún Shū 荀淑, courtesy name Jìhé 季和,
was a native of Yǐngyīn 潁陰, Yǐngchuān 潁川.
Those he selected from among the commoners and herdsmen,
and from among the low-ranking officials who handled documents and knives,
all became outstanding talents.
He was recommended as 'upright and proper,'
and appointed as the chancellor of the Marquis of Lǎngl陵,
where he spread his influence.
Zhōng Hào 鍾皓, courtesy name Jìmíng 季明,
was a native of Chángshè 長社, Yǐngchuān 潁川. His father and grandfather were famous for their utmost virtue.
Hào 皓 upheld the noble character of his family,
was appointed as the magistrate of Línlǜ 林慮,
but did not take office.
Although his official position was insufficient,
his heavenly endowed virtue was abundant."
It says:
"Lord Xún's 荀 clarity of understanding is hard to surpass,
Lord Zhōng's 鍾 supreme virtue is worthy of emulation."
The *Biographies of Distinguished Worthies Within the Seas* states:
"The elders of Yǐngchuān 潁川,
who were emulated by all within the seas, were:
Chén Zhìshū 陳穉叔 of Dìnglíng 定陵, Xún Shū 荀淑 of Yǐngyīn 潁陰, and Zhōng Hào 鍾皓 of Chángshè 長社.
Lǐ Yīng 李膺, the Vice Director of the Palace, revered these three gentlemen,
and often said:
'Lord Xún's 荀 clarity of understanding is hard to surpass,
and Chén 陳 and Zhōng's 鍾 supreme virtue is worthy of emulation.'"
Chén Tàiqiū paid a visit to Xún Lǎngl陵,
who was poor and frugal, without servants.
The *Biography of Chén Shí* says:
"Shí, courtesy name Zhònggōng,
was from Xǔchāng in Yǐngchuān.
He served as Magistrate of Wénxǐ and
Chief of Tàiqiū,
where his virtuous influence spread widely."
He then sent Yuánfāng as general.
The *Records of Worthy Predecessors* says:
"Chén Jì, courtesy name Yuánfāng,
was Shí's eldest son.
His virtue was extraordinary and detached from the common world.
His lofty reputation rivaled that of Shí,
and his younger brother Chén was also worthy of being paired with them.
Every time the headquarters of a governor summoned them,
the gifts of lamb and geese came in droves.
The world called them
'The Three Gentlemen,'
and portraits of them were displayed in all the cities."
Jìfāng followed behind with a staff.
Chángwén was still young
and was carried in the chariot.
Upon arrival,
Xún sent Shūcí to answer the door,
Címíng served the wine,
and the remaining six dragons went down to eat.
Zhāng Fán's *Annals of the Hàn* says:
"Shū had eight sons:
Jiǎn, Kūn,
Jìng, Tāo,
Wāng, Shuǎng,
Sù, and Fū.
Shū lived in Xīháo Hamlet.
County Magistrate Yuàn Kāng said,
'In the past, Emperor Gāoyáng had eight talented sons,'
and so he named the hamlet Gāoyáng Hamlet.
The people of the time called them the Eight Dragons."
Wén Ruò was also young
and sat with chopsticks before him.
At that time, the Grand Historian reported:
"A true man is traveling east."
Tán Dàoluán's *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Chén Zhònggōng followed his sons and nephews to visit the Xún father and sons.
At that time, virtue stars gathered,
and the Grand Historian reported:
'Worthy men have gathered within five hundred *lǐ*.'"
A guest asked Chén Jìfāng:
*Hǎinèi Xiānxián Zhuàn* says:
"Chén Chén, courtesy name Jìfāng,
was truly the youngest son.
He had broad and profound talent and knowledge.
He was summoned by the Sīkōng's office and the imperial carriage,
but he did not accept."
"Your father, Tàiqiū,
what merit or virtue does he have
How did [he] bear the reputation of such importance in the world?"
Jì Fāng said:
"My father is like a cassia tree growing on the side of Mount Tài,
with ten thousand *rèn* of height above,
and immeasurable depths below;
above, it is moistened by sweet dew,
below, it is nourished by deep springs.
At such a time,
how would the cassia tree know the height of Mount Tài,
or the depth of the deep springs,
and not know whether it has merit or not!"
Chén Yuánfāng's son, Chángwén, had outstanding talent.
The "Book of Wèi" says:
"Chén Qún, style name Chángwén,
his grandfather was Shí,
once said to his clan members:
'This child will surely bring prosperity to our clan.'
When he grew up,
he had knowledge and measure.
Those he favored
were all associates of his father."
and Jì Fāng's son, Xiàoxiān.
The "Genealogy of the Chén Clan" says:
"Chén's son, Zhōng,
style name Xiàoxiān.
He was summoned by the province but did not accept."
Each discussed the merits and virtues of their father,
and the dispute could not be resolved,
He consulted Tàiqiū.
Tàiqiū said:
"It's difficult for Yuánfāng to be the elder brother,
it's difficult for Jìfāng to be the younger brother."
One version reads
"It's difficult for Yuánfāng to be the younger brother,
it's difficult for Jìfāng to be the elder brother."
Xún Jùbó traveled far to visit a friend who was ill.
The "Xún Family Chronicle" says:
"Jùbó,
was a man of the time of Emperor Huán of the Hàn Dynasty.
He also came from Yǐngchuān,
but his origins and end are not known in detail."
He encountered Hú bandits attacking the commandery.
The friend said to Jùbó:
"I am going to die now,
you may leave!" Jùbó said:
"I came from afar to see you,
and you tell me to leave;
to abandon righteousness in order to seek life,
how could that be what Xún Jùbó would do?" When the bandits arrived,
they said to Jùbó:
"The great army has arrived,
the entire commandery is empty,
what kind of man are you,
that you dare to stay alone?"
Jùbó said:
"My friend is ill,
I cannot bear to abandon him.
I would rather give my own life in place of my friend's."
The bandits said to each other,
"We are unrighteous men,
yet we have entered a righteous country!" They then withdrew their troops and returned,
and the entire commandery was spared.
Huá Xīn treated his younger relatives with great strictness.
Even in the private chambers,
it was as solemn as a court ceremony.
The *Wèi Zhì* says:
"Xīn's courtesy name was Zǐyú,
he was from Gāotáng in Píngyuán."
The *Wèi Lüè* says:
"During the reign of Emperor Líng, he, Bǐng Yuán of Běihǎi,
and Guǎn Níng all studied together and were very close.
At the time, the three of them were known as 'one dragon.'
Xīn was said to be the dragon's head,
Níng the dragon's belly,
and Yuán the dragon's tail."
Chén Yuánfāng and his brother freely practiced the way of gentleness and love, and within the two gates [of their homes],
both maintained a harmonious and peaceful course.
Guǎn Níng and Huá Xīn were once weeding vegetables together in the garden.
The *Fù Zǐ* says:
"Níng's courtesy name was Yòu'ān,
he was from Zhūxū in Běihǎi,
He was a descendant of Guǎn Zhòng (管仲), the chancellor of Qí.
They saw a piece of gold on the ground.
Guǎn treated it no differently than clods of earth and stones when he swung his hoe.
Huá picked it up and threw it away.
Once, they were reading together at the same mat.
Someone in a carriage with ceremonial hats and robes passed by the door.
Níng continued reading as before.
Xīn put down his book and went out to watch.
Níng cut the mat and separated his seat, saying:
"You are not my friend."
The *Wèi Lüè* says:
"Níng was quiet and tranquil in his youth.
He often laughed at Bǐng Yuán (邴原) and Huá Zǐyú (華子魚) for having intentions to seek officialdom."
When Xīn became Minister of Education,
he wrote a memorial recommending Níng.
Níng laughed upon hearing it, saying:
"Zǐyú originally wanted to be an old official,
so he glorifies it."
Wáng Lǎng (王朗) often praised Huá Xīn for his discernment and judgment.
The *Wèi Shū* says:
"Lǎng's courtesy name was Jǐngxīng (景興).
He was a native of Tán (郯) in Dōnghǎi (東海),
and served as Minister of Education in Wèi." Xīn's là day,
The *Lǐjì* says:
"The Son of Heaven performs the great là sacrifice eight times.
Yíqí (伊耆) was the first to perform the là.
Là means 'to seek'.
In the twelfth month of the year,
to gather all things and seek to enjoy them."
The "Essential Meanings of the Five Classics" says:
"The Three Dynasties named the Là differently:
The Xia called it Jiāpíng,
the Yin called it Qīngsì,
the Zhou called it Dàlà,
and collectively it was called Là."
Zhāng Liàng, a scholar of the Jin dynasty, argued:
"Là means
to gather all things and seek to enjoy them,
and at the end of the year to rest the old and give the people respite.
Là means
to sacrifice to the ancestral temple and the five sacrifices.
The "Commentary" says:
'Là
means to connect.'
Sacrificing is the juncture of the old and the new.
Since the Qin and Han dynasties,
the day after Là is called Zhù Suì (Wishing the Year Well),
a saying passed down from ancient times." He often gathered his nephews and nieces for feasts and drinks,
and Wáng also learned to do this.
Someone told Zhāng Huá about this matter,
and Zhāng said:
"Wáng's learning from Huá
is all superficial,
and it is because of this that he strays further."
Wáng Yǐn's "Book of Jin" says:
"Zhāng Huá, courtesy name Màoxiān,
He was a person from Fànyáng.
He was promoted several times, reaching the position of Sīkōng,
but was harmed by Zhào Wáng Lún."
Huá Xīn and Wáng Lǎng were both on a boat fleeing from disaster.
There was a person who wanted to attach himself to them,
but Xīn immediately found it difficult.
Lǎng said,
"Fortunately, there is still room,
why is it not permissible?"
Later, the bandits chased after them,
and Wáng wanted to abandon the person he had brought along.
Xīn said,
"The reason I was originally doubtful
was precisely for this reason.
Since we have already accepted his reliance on us,
how can we abandon him in a time of urgency?"
So he carried and rescued him as before.
The world used this to determine the superiority or inferiority of Huá and Wáng.
Huá Qiáo's "Genealogy Preface" says:
"Xīn was the magistrate of Xiàguī.
When the Hàn court was in turmoil,
he and six or seven like-minded gentlemen such as Zhèng Tài withdrew from the world.
They departed from Wǔ Pass,
and on the road, they encountered a solitary man traveling alone,
who wished to join them.
They all compassionately agreed.
Xīn alone said,
"No.
Now we are in danger,
good fortune, misfortune, worry, and harm
are all the same.
To receive it now without reason,
not knowing its meaning,
if there is advancement or retreat,
can we abandon it midway?"
The others could not bear to,
and finally went with him.
This is like a man falling into a well on the road;
everyone wants to abandon him.
Xīn then said,
"We have already come together,
it would be unrighteous to abandon him."
In the end, they returned together,
rescued him, and then parted."
Wáng Xiáng served his stepmother, Zhū Fūren, with great care.
The *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* says:
"Xiáng, styled Xiūzhēng,
was from Lángyé, Línyí."
The *Xiáng Shìjiā* says:
"Xiáng's father was Róng,
who married a Xūe woman from Gāopíng,
and she gave birth to Xiáng.
He remarried with a Zhū woman from Lújiāng,
who gave birth to Lǎn."
The *Jìn Yángqiū* says:
"His stepmother frequently slandered Xiáng,
repeatedly treating Xiáng unreasonably.
His younger brother, Lǎn, always stayed with Xiáng.
She also cruelly abused Xiáng's wife.
Lǎn's wife would also hasten to share the work.
When his mother fell ill,
and the weather was severely cold with ice frozen,
his mother desired fresh fish.
Xiáng undressed and was about to break the ice to seek it,
when someone happened to urinate in the ice,
and fish came out."
Xiāo Guǎngjì's "Biography of a Filial Son" says:
"Xiáng's stepmother suddenly wanted roasted yellow sparrows.
Xiáng thought it would be difficult to obtain them immediately.
In a short while,
several dozen yellow sparrows flew into her tent.
Whatever his mother needed,
he would personally exert himself,
and there was nothing he could not obtain.
His sincerity was so great."
At home there was a plum tree,
which bore exceptionally good fruit.
His mother always made him guard it.
Once, a wind and rain suddenly came,
Xiáng hugged the tree and wept.
Xiāo Guǎngjì's "Biography of a Filial Son" says:
"Xiáng's stepmother had a plum tree in the courtyard,
which had just begun to bear fruit.
He made Xiáng watch the birds and sparrows during the day,
and chase away the rats at night.
One night,
a great wind and rain arrived,
Xiáng embraced (his mother) and wept until dawn,
and his mother saw him and felt saddened."
Xiáng once slept in a separate bed,
his mother went by herself to strike him in the dark,
but Xiáng happened to get up privately,
and only struck the bedding.
After she returned,
knowing that his mother's resentment had not ceased,
therefore he knelt before her and requested to die.
Thereupon his mother was awakened (to her senses),
and loved him as her own son.
Yú Yù in the "Book of Jìn" said:
"Xiáng, because of his stepmother's reasons,
gradually declined to serve (in office).
Approaching the age of sixty,
the Inspector Lǚ Qián summoned him to be a Regional Assessor (bié jià),
at the time people sang of him saying:
'The peace of Hǎi Yí,
truly relies on Wáng Xiáng;
the state is not empty,
it is the merit of the Regional Assessor!'
He was repeatedly promoted to Grand Protector."
King Wén of Jìn praised Ruǎn Sìzōng for being extremely cautious,
every time he spoke with him,
His words were all profound and far-reaching;
he never praised or criticized people.
The *Wèi Shū* says:
"Wén Wáng's taboo name was Zhāo,
styled Zǐshàng,
the second son of Xuān Dì."
The *Wèi Shì Chūnqiū* says:
"Ruǎn Jí, styled Sìzōng,
was a native of Wèishì in Chénliú,
the son of Ruǎn Yǔ. He was broad-minded and unrestrained,
not bound by etiquette and customs.
Wáng Chǎng, the Inspector of Yǎn Province, requested to meet him,
but was unable to speak with him all day.
Chǎng was ashamed and sighed,
considering himself unable to fathom him.
His mouth did not discuss affairs;
he was naturally lofty and transcendent."
Lǐ Kāng's *Family Admonitions* says:
"In the past, I once sat in attendance upon the late Emperor,
when three Chief Clerks were present together.
As they were about to take their leave,
the Emperor said:
'To be an official, one should be honest,
one should be cautious, one should be diligent.
Cultivate these three,
and what worry is there of not governing well?'
They all received the imperial instruction.
The Emperor turned to us and said:
"If one absolutely must leave,
which of these three should be prioritized?"
Someone replied:
"Purity (qīng) is certainly fundamental."
The emperor asked me again, and I replied:
"The ways of purity and caution (shèn)
are mutually dependent for success.
If one absolutely must choose,
caution is paramount."
The emperor said:
"What you say makes sense.
Who in recent times can you name who was truly cautious?"
I then mentioned the former Grand Commandant Xún Jǐngqiàn,
the Secretary Dǒng Zhòngdá, and the Palace Attendant Wáng Gōngzhòng.
The emperor said:
"These people
were mild and respectful morning and evening,
and dutiful in their responsibilities;
each was cautious in his own way.
But the most cautious person in the world,
isn't it Ruǎn Sìzōng?
Every time I spoke with him,
the conversation touched on abstruse and distant topics,
but he never commented on current affairs
or judged people.
Can he be considered supremely cautious?"
Wáng Róng said:
"I lived with Jī Kāng for twenty years
He never showed any signs of joy or anger."
The preface to "Kāng Jí" says:
"Kāng, styled Shūyè,
was from Zhì in Qiáo Commandery."
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" says:
"Jī's original surname was Xī,
and his ancestors moved to Shàngyú to avoid a feud, and then moved to Zhì County in Qiáo Commandery.
Because they came from Kuàijī,
they took one branch of the country's name,
and its pronunciation was the same as the original Xī."
Yú Yù's "Jìn Shū" says:
"There is Mount Jī in Zhì,
and they lived near it,
so they took it as their surname."
"Kāng Bié Zhuàn" says:
"Kāng was tolerant of dirt and hid imperfections,
his likes and dislikes were not argued in his heart,
and his joy and anger were not displayed on his face.
Wáng Jùnchōng, whom he knew, was in Xiāngchéng,
having met hundreds of times,
he never saw him raise his voice or blush.
This is also a model of balanced behavior,
and a superior achievement in human relations."
"Wénzhāng Xùlù" says:
"Kāng was promoted to Lángzhōng because he was the son-in-law of the chief of the Chánglè Pavilion of the Wèi dynasty,
and was appointed as a Zhōngsàn Dàfū."
Wáng Róng and Hé Jiǎo both suffered great funerals at the same time,
Both were known for their filial piety.
Wáng Róng supported himself with a chicken bone frame
and his mourning included weeping and complete rituals.
The *Jin Zhū Gōng Zàn* states:
"Róng, whose courtesy name was Jùnchōng,
was a native of Lángyé,
and belonged to the clan of Grand Protector Xiáng.
When Emperor Wén was assisting in the government,
Zhōng Huì recommended him, saying:
'Péi Kǎi is clear and insightful,
and Wáng Róng is concise and essential.'
Both were immediately summoned as clerks.
When the Jin ascended the throne,
he was repeatedly promoted to Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
For his merit in pacifying Wú,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānfēng."
The *Jìn Yángqiū* states:
"Róng served as the Inspector of Yùzhōu.
When he encountered the mourning for his mother,
he was extremely filial.
He did not adhere to ritual restrictions;
he drank wine and ate meat,
and sometimes watched chess games.
Yet his appearance was emaciated
and he needed a staff to stand up.
At that time, Hé Qiào of Rǔnán,
also a famous scholar,
maintained himself with ritual propriety.
In great sorrow,
he measures out rice to eat,
yet he is haggard and emaciated from grief,
not up to the standard of Róng also."
Wǔ Dì said to Liú Zhòngxióng:
Wáng Yǐn's *Jin Shu* says:
"Liú Yì, zi Zhòngxióng,
was a native of Yè in Dōnglái,
a descendant of the King Jǐng of Chéngyáng during the Hàn dynasty.
He was upright, honest, pure, and principled.
When he saw something wrong,
he would definitely comment on it.
High officials and great men
feared him at the mere mention of his name.
He resided in Yángpíng as a guest.
The Prefect Dù Shù appointed him as Chief Clerk,
and he purged over three hundred corrupt officials from the prefecture.
The Three Wèi generally said:
'We only hear about Chief Clerk Liú,
and not about Prefect Dù.'
He was successively promoted to Palace Secretary,
and then Imperial Inspector of the Capital."
"Do you often visit Wáng and Hé?
I heard that Hé's mourning is excessively grievous,
which makes people worry about him."
Zhòngxióng said:
"Although Hé Qiáo observes all the rites,
his spirit is not diminished;
Wáng Róng 王戎, although not complete in ritual propriety,
was nonetheless emaciated from grief, to the point of being skin and bones.
Your subject believes that Hé Qiáo 和嶠 was filial in life,
and Wáng Róng 王戎 was filial in death.
Your Majesty should not be worried about Qiáo 嶠,
but should be worried about Róng 戎."
*Jìn Yáng Qiū* 《晉陽秋》 says:
"Emperor Shìzǔ 世祖 valued Róng 戎 because of this conversation."
The Prince of Liáng 梁王 and the Prince of Zhào 趙王,
Zhū Fèng's 朱鳳 *Jìn Shū* 《晉書》 says:
"Emperor Xuāndì's 宣帝 wife, Lady Zhāng 張, gave birth to Liáng Xiào Wáng Tóng 梁孝王彤,
styled Zǐhuī 子徽,
whose position reached Grand Protector.
Lady Huán 桓 gave birth to Zhào Wáng Lún 趙王倫,
styled Zǐyí 子彝,
whose position reached Prime Minister."
Being close relatives of the state, they were highly valued at the time.
Lord Péi 裴, the Director,
in his *Zàn* 贊 (Eulogies/Appreciations) of the Dukes of Jìn 晉 says:
"Péi Kǎi 裴楷, styled Shūzé 叔則,
was from Wénxǐ 聞喜 in Hédōng 河東.
He was the younger brother of the descendant of Sīkōng Xiù 司空秀.
His father, Huī 徽,
was the Governor of Jìzhōu 冀州,
and possessed outstanding insight.
Kǎi 楷 was particularly well-versed in the meaning of the *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes).
He was repeatedly promoted to Prefect of Hénán 河南,
died."
As the Director of the Secretariat,
every year he requested several million in tax money from the two states
to provide for the poor among his relatives.
Someone ridiculed him, saying:
"Why do you beg for things to bestow favors?"
Péi said:
"To diminish the surplus
and supplement the deficiency
is the way of Heaven."
The *Record of Famous Gentlemen* says:
"Kǎi's conduct, in taking and giving,
followed his heart's inclination.
Though praise and blame might arrive,
he met them calmly.
All were of this kind."
Wáng Róng said:
"The Grand Protector lived during the Zhèngshǐ period
and was not among the eloquent.
But when you spoke with him,
his reasoning was balanced, pure, and profound.
Could it be that his virtue overshadowed his words!"
The *Annals of Jìn* says:
"Xiáng possessed fine virtue and conduct from a young age."
Wáng Ānfēng encountered hardship
and his filial piety surpassed others.
Péi Lìng went to offer condolences and said:
"If a single outburst of grief could truly harm a person,
"If one is overly restrained and placid, one cannot avoid the criticism of destroying one's nature."
The *Qū Lǐ* (Book of Rites) says:
"The rites for mourning
require that emaciation not be visibly affected,
and that sight and hearing not decline.
If one cannot bear the mourning,
then one is comparable to being unkind and unfilial."
The *Xiào Jīng* (Classic of Filial Piety) says:
"Emaciation without destroying one's nature
is the teaching of the sages."
Wáng Róng's 王戎 father, Hún 渾, had a fine reputation,
and his official position reached Governor of Liángzhōu 涼州.
The *Shì Yǔ* (Tales of the World) says:
"Hún 渾, courtesy name Chángyuán 長原,
possessed talent and reputation.
He served as an Attendant Secretary,
and Governor of Liángzhōu 涼州."
When Hún 渾 died,
the righteous officials of the nine commanderies he had governed,
cherishing his virtue and kindness,
joined together to offer funeral gifts of several million [coins],
but Róng 戎 refused them all.
Yú Yù's 虞預 *Jìn Shū* (Book of Jin) says:
"Róng 戎 gained a prominent reputation because of this."
Liú Dàozhēn 劉道真 once worked as a convict laborer.
The *Jìn Bǎi Guān Míng* (Names of Jin Dynasty Officials) says:
"Liú Bǎo 劉寶, courtesy name Dàozhēn 道真,
was from Gāopíng 高平.
"Those sentenced to penal servitude were called
'zuìyì zuòzhě' (罪役作者), those who work in penal servitude."
Fúfēng (扶風) Prince, Wáng Jùn (王駿), Yú Yù (虞預) in
the *Book of Jin* says:
"Jùn's courtesy name was Zǐzāng (子臧).
He was the seventeenth son of Emperor Xuān (宣帝), and he loved learning
and was extremely filial."
The *Zàns* (贊, Eulogies) of the Princes of Jin states:
"Jùn, at the age of eight, became a Gentleman-in-Attendance (散騎常侍),
and attended Wei Qíwáng (魏齊王) in lectures.
When Jin received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Fúfēng (扶風王),
garrisoned Guānzhōng (關中),
and his governance was most excellent.
He died and was posthumously granted the title of Prince Wǔ (武王).
The people of the western lands missed him,
and whenever they saw his inscription and eulogy on his stele,
they would all bow and weep.
Such was the legacy of his love."
He was redeemed with five hundred bolts of cloth,
and subsequently employed as an Attendant Gentleman of the Interior (從事中郎).
At that time, this was considered a laudable action.
Wáng Píngzǐ (王平子), Húmǔ Yànguó (胡毋彥國), and others,
all considered unrestrained behavior as "dá (達)" [wise],
some even went naked.
The *Zàns* (贊, Eulogies) of the Princes of Jin states:
"Wáng Chéng (王澄), courtesy name Píngzǐ (平子),
had profound understanding,
and was the Inspector of Jīngzhōu."
The "List of Émigrés of the Yǒngjiā Era" states:
"Húmǔ Fǔzhī, style name Yànguó,
was a native of Fénggāo in Mount Tài,
and was the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu."
Wáng Yǐn's "Book of Jìn" says:
"At the end of the Wei dynasty, Ruǎn Jí
was fond of wine and unrestrained,
showing his head and disheveled hair,
naked and sitting with legs spread.
Later, aristocratic young men such as Ruǎn Zhān, Wáng Chéng,
Xiè Kūn, and Húmǔ Fǔzhī,
all followed the example of Jí,
claiming to have grasped the essence of the Great Way.
Therefore, they removed their headscarves,
took off their clothes,
exposed their ugliness,
and behaved like beasts.
The worst were called 'unfettered' (通 *tōng*),
and the next worst were called 'enlightened' (達 *dá*)."
Yuè Guǎng laughed and said:
"There is happiness within the realm of moral principles and social norms (名教 *míngjiào*),
why do you act like that!"
When Xī Gōng encountered the chaos of the Yǒngjiā period,
he was very poor and hungry in his hometown.
The villagers, because of his reputation and virtue,
shared food to nourish him.
Duke often took his brother's son, Mài,
and his sister's son, the two young boys, Zhōu Yì, to eat.
The villagers said:
"Everyone is hungry and in distress.
Given your virtue,
they want to help you together,
but I'm afraid you can't afford to keep everyone alive."
Thereupon, the Duke went to eat alone,
always holding rice in his cheeks with chopsticks
and returning to spit it out to the two boys.
Later, they both survived
and crossed the river together.
"Separate Biography of Xī Jiàn" says:
"Jiàn's courtesy name was Dàohuī,
he was a man from Jīnxiāng in Gāopíng.
He was a descendant of Xī Lǜ, Grand Commandant during the Hàn Dynasty.
He was upright from a young age,
devoted to studying the classics,
and famous for his refined scholarship.
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
the world was in great chaos,
with famine stretching as far as the eye could see.
People of official rank and below
all cut into their own resources to supply Jiàn.
Emperor Yuán summoned him to be Lieutenant General,
and he was promoted to Minister of Works
and Grand Commandant."
"The Book of the Restoration" says:
Jiàn Xiōng's son, Mài,
styled Sīyuǎn,
possessed talent and strategies to manage the world.
He successively advanced to positions such as Shǎofǔ (Junior Treasurer) and
Zhōng Hùjūn (Central Protector of the Army).
When Xī Gōng died,
Yì was magistrate of Shàn County.
He resigned from his post and returned home,
placing a straw mat by the head of the ancestral spirit bed,
observing mourning in his heart for a full three years.
The "Zhōu Family Genealogy" states:
"Yì's style name was Zǐqīng,
a person from Chén Commandery.
His grandfather was Yì,
Grand Administrator of Shànggǔ.
His father was Yōu,
a Consultant to the General of Chariots and Cavalry.
He served as magistrate of Shàn,
Governor of Qīng Province,
and Shǎofǔ Qīng (Minister of the Junior Treasury),
dying at the age of sixty-four."
Gù Róng was in Luòyáng.
Once, responding to someone's invitation,
he noticed the expression of desire on the face of the person serving roasted meat,
so he stopped his own eating and gave it to him.
Those sitting with him ridiculed him.
Róng said,
"How can someone hold it all day,
and not know its taste?"
Later, encountering turmoil and crossing the river,
whenever he was in danger,
there was always someone to his left and right.
Asking the reason for this,
it turned out to be the person who prepared the roasted meat.
The *Wénshì Zhuàn* (Biographies of Scholars) says:
"Róng, zi Yànxiān,
was from Wú Commandery.
His ancestors were collateral descendants of the King Gōujiàn of Yuè,
enfeoffed in Gù Township,
and their descendants thus took Gù as their surname,
for generations a prominent family in Wú.
His grandfather was Yōng,
the Chancellor of Wú.
His father was Mù,
the Governor of Yídū.
Róng was intelligent and quick-witted from a young age,
with a spirited and outstanding appearance,
and served as Chief Justice of the Court of Justice.
Once, in the palace, he was drinking with his colleagues,
and seeing that the person preparing the roasted meat was different from ordinary servants,
he cut off some roasted meat to feed him.
Later, Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne,
and his son, as General of the Central Guard,
forced Róng to serve as his Chief Secretary.
When Lún was executed,
Róng was also arrested.
There were more than ten people in total who were executed.
Someone tried to save Róng.
They asked the reason.
They said:
"He is a favored official in a certain province."
Róng then understood and sighed, saying:
"The kindness of a single meal,
I do not forget even now,
how can the words of the ancients be false!"
Zǔ Guānglù (祖光祿) was orphaned and poor at a young age,
and was extremely filial.
He often cooked and prepared food for his mother himself.
Wáng Yǐn's (王隱) *Jin Shu* (晉書) says:
"Zǔ Nà (祖納), zi Shìyán (士言),
was from Fányáng Qiú (范陽遒),
and for nine generations his family had been recommended as Xiàolián (孝廉)."
Zǔ Nà (祖納) had three elder brothers from different mothers,
and he was most noted for his virtuous conduct,
and was skilled in pure conversation.
He served as the Middle Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and Minister of the Court of Justice.
He took refuge in the South of the Yangtze River.
Wēn Qiào (溫嶠) recommended him as Grand Master of the Palace (Guānglù Dàfū, 光祿大夫)."
Wáng Píngběi (王平北) heard of his excellent reputation
and sent him two female servants as gifts,
and subsequently took him on as a Gentleman of the Household (Zhōngláng, 中郎).
The *Wáng Yì Bié Zhuàn* (王乂別傳) says:
Ǎi Zì, courtesy name Shūyuán,
was from Lángyé, Línyí.
At that time, Shǔ had just been pacified,
and two generals were causing trouble.
Emperor Wéndì went west to Cháng'ān,
and therefore summoned him to be the Chancellor's Sīmǎ,
promoted him to Grand Secretary,
and sent him out to supervise the military affairs of Yōu Province,
as General Who Pacifies the North.
Someone jokingly said to him:
"The price of a male slave is twice that of a female slave."
Ǎi Zì said,
"Why must Bǎilǐ Xī be considered lighter than the five ram skins?"
*Biographies of the Worthies of Chǔ* says:
"Bǎilǐ Xī's courtesy name was Jǐngbó,
and he was a person from Chǔ.
In his youth, he served in Yú
as a senior official.
When Jìn wanted to borrow a route through Yú to attack Guó,
he advised against it, but was not listened to,
so Xī left."
*Shuō Yuàn* says:
"Duke Mù of Qín sent merchants to load salt in Yú.
The merchants bought Bǎilǐ Xī for five ram skins.
Duke Mù inspected the salt
and was surprised that the cattle were fat.
He asked the reason,
and they replied:
"Eating and drinking at regular times,
not indulging excessively,
this is how one becomes healthy."
The Duke ordered the officials to bathe and put on ceremonial robes.
Gōngsūn Zhī yielded his ministerial position,
and was called the "Five Ram Minister."
Zhōu Zhèn was dismissed from his position as Governor of Línchuān Commandery and returned to the capital,
before he could reside in his official dwelling,
he moored at the Qingxī Isle.
*Yǒngjiā Exiles' Names* says:
"Zhèn's courtesy name was Kāngshí,
he was a native of Wèishì in Chénliú.
His grandfather was Hé,
former Magistrate of Gù'ān.
His father was Zhèn,
a Chief Clerk in the Ministry of Works."
*Zhongxing Book* says:
"Zhèn was pure, frugal, and had few desires,
wherever he was, he achieved extraordinary accomplishments."
The Prime Minister Wáng went to see him.
*Prime Minister's Biography* says:
"Wáng Dǎo's courtesy name was Màohóng,
he was from Lángyá.
His grandfather was Lǎn,
known for his virtue.
His father was Cái,
an Attendant Censor.
Dǎo gained fame at a young age,
His family circumstances were poor and simple,
yet he was content and happy, delighting in the Way,
and never burdened by worldly concerns."
At that time, it was the summer month,
and a sudden heavy rain arrived.
The boat was very small,
and also leaked badly,
so there was almost no place to sit.
Wáng said:
"How can anyone surpass [Hú] Wēi's integrity
in this situation!"
He was immediately appointed as the administrator of Wúxīng Commandery.
The "Annals of Jìnyáng" say:
"Hú Wēi, styled Bóhǔ,
was a native of Huáinán.
His father, Zhì, was known for his loyalty and integrity.
When Zhì was serving in Jīngzhōu,
Wēi traveled from the capital to visit him.
When he was about to return home,
Zhì gave Wēi a bolt of silk.
Wēi knelt and said:
'You, sir, are pure and lofty,
where did you get this?'
Zhì said:
'This is from the remainder of my official salary,
so I am giving it to you as travel provisions.'
Wēi accepted it and left.
Whenever he reached an inn,
He himself released the donkey, gathered firewood, and cooked a meal.
After eating,
he continued to travel along the road with the other travelers.
Zhì's subordinate commander secretly brought grain to intercept him,
and so he became his companion.
He assisted with and managed everything.
He also offered a small amount of food.
Wēi suspected him
and secretly questioned him,
and then learned that he was indeed the commander.
He thanked him and sent him away.
Later, he reported this to Zhì.
Zhì had the commander flogged one hundred times
and removed his name from the official rolls.
Such was the integrity and prudence of father and son.
Later, when Wēi was in Xúzhōu,
Shìzǔ granted him an audience
and discussed border affairs and his life with him.
The emperor praised his father's integrity
and then said to Wēi,
"Whose integrity is greater, yours or your father's?"
He replied, "My integrity is not as great as my father's."
The emperor said, "In what way is he superior to you?"
He replied, "My father's integrity was such that he feared people would know about it,
my integrity is such that I fear people will *not* know about it,
therefore I am far inferior."
Dèng Yōu, when he first fled from disaster,
abandoned his own son on the road
Quán Dìzǐ (全弟子, Complete Disciples).
《Jìnyáng Qiū》 (晉陽秋, The Annals of Jìnyáng) says:
"Yōu, courtesy name Bó Dào (伯道),
was from Xiānglíng (襄陵) in Píngyáng (平陽).
At the age of seven, he lost his parents and grandparents,
and maintained proper decorum for nine years.
His nature was pure, cautious, fair, and simple."
Dèng Càn's (鄧粲)《Jìn Jì》 (晉紀, Records of the Jìn Dynasty) says:
"During the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) period,
Yōu was captured by Shí Lè (石勒).
He was summoned for an audience, placed under his command, and spoken to.
Shí Lè was pleased with him, and had him sit and eat a meal.
Yōu's carriage was parked
with its wheels adjacent to those of a barbarian.
The barbarian accidentally started a fire, burning the wagon camp.
Shí Lè's officials investigated the barbarian,
and the barbarian falsely accused Yōu.
Yōu, realizing that there was no point in arguing,
said,
'Earlier, I was making porridge for an old woman,
and the fire spread accidentally,
a crime deserving ten thousand deaths.'
Shí Lè, knowing this, released him.
The barbarian who falsely accused him was deeply grateful to Yōu,
gave him his donkeys and horses,
and escorted him, allowing him to escape."
Wáng Yǐn's (王隱)《Jìn Shū》 (晉書, Book of Jìn) says:
"Yōu, because of the long distance,
He destroyed his cart,
and used oxen and horses to carry his wife and children to rebel.
The bandits then plundered his oxen and horses.
Yōu said to his wife:
"My younger brother died early,
leaving only a son.
Now, if we walk,
carrying both children will surely lead to their deaths.
It's better to abandon our own child,
and carry the orphaned child.
We can still have children later."
His wife agreed."
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Yōu abandoned his child in the grass.
The child cried and called after him,
but by dusk, he could no longer reach him.
The next day, Yōu tied the child to a tree and left,
then crossed the river.
He eventually became *Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè*, and died. His disciple Suī observed three years of mourning for Yōu according to the Qíshuāi ritual."
After crossing the river,
he took a concubine,
whom he greatly favored.
After many years, he inquired about her background.
The concubine explained in detail that she was a Northerner who had suffered in the chaos,
and she recalled her parents' names.
It turned out she was Yōu's niece.
Yōu had always had virtue and good deeds,
and his words and actions were without blemish.
Hearing of it, he grieved and hated it for the rest of his life,
and consequently never again kept concubines.
Wáng Chángyù was a cautious and obedient man,
serving his parents with utmost filial piety and providing them with comfort.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* (Book of the Restoration) says:
"Wáng Yuè, zi (style name) Chángyù,
was the eldest son of the Chancellor Dǎo.
He rose in office to Attendant Gentleman of the Inner Secretariat."
The Chancellor was always pleased to see Chángyù,
but always angry to see Jìngyù.
The *Wénzì Zhì* (Record of Writing) says:
"Wáng Tián, zi Jìngyù,
was the second son of Dǎo.
He was unconventional and unconstrained in his youth,
disliking study and valuing martial pursuits,
and was not valued by Dǎo.
He rose to General of the Central Army.
He possessed many talents and skills,
and was skilled in clerical script,
and was known with Jìyáng Jiāng Bīn for his skill in Weiqi (Go)."
When Chángyù spoke with the Chancellor,
he always made caution and discretion his starting point.
When the Chancellor returned to the Terrace (referring to his office),
and when he departed,
he (Chángyù) never failed to see him off to the back of his carriage.
He always shared in the task of managing the trunks and boxes with Madam Cáo.
After Chángyù died,
when the Chancellor returned to the Terrace,
After boarding the carriage,
she cried all the way to the gate of the platform.
Cáo Fūrén made a casket,
sealed it, but couldn't bear to open it.
The *Wáng Shì Pǔ* states:
"Dǎo married the daughter of Cáo Sháo of Péngchéng,
named Shū."
When Attendant 侍 Húan 常 heard someone speak of Shēn Gōng,
he would always say:
"This man already has a long-standing reputation,
and the late worthies praised him,
furthermore, he was a close friend of my late father,
it is not appropriate to criticize him."
*The Unofficial Biography of Huán Yí* states:
"Yí, courtesy name Mào Lún,
was a native of Lóngkàng in Qiáo Prefecture,
and a tenth-generation descendant of the Han official, Huán Róng.
His father, Yǐng,
had a high reputation.
Yí was orphaned young,
but had clear and bright discernment.
To avoid the chaos, he crossed the Yangtze River,
and successively rose to the position of Attendant侍 in Ordinary 騎常."
The monk Fǎshēn,
his lay surname is unknown,
was likely a descendant of a scholarly family.
His virtues and lofty reputation
spread throughout Shāndōng.
He was a disciple of Master Liú of Zhōngzhōu.
During the Yǒngjiā Rebellion,
he took refuge in the lands of Yáng.
He resided in the capital city,
inwardly upholding the Dharma principles,
and outwardly exemplifying admirable conduct,
a Dharma Master who propagated the Way.
Because of his practice of compassion, purity,
and intolerance for worldly affairs,
he examined and settled in the 𡵙 Mountain, two hundred *lǐ* east of Shàn County,
where he lived with more than ten companions,
dwelling loftily in serenity.
Zhī Dàolín admired his demeanor
and, in a letter to a Korean Daoist,
praised his virtue.
He passed away in the mountains at the age of seventy-nine."
Duke Yǔ rode a Delú horse.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Yǔ Liàng, *zì* Yuánguī,
was a native of Yānlíng in Yǐngchuān,
and the eldest brother of Empress Míngmù.
He was refined, elegant, virtuous, and measured.
People at the time compared him to Xiàhóu Tàichū
and Chén Chángwén.
Attending his father, Chēn,
he sought refuge in Kuàijī.
Dignified and upright,
Yán Dànzhī 嚴憚之 was a man from the commandery.
Those who were granted an audience with him
were only a few people.
He was successively promoted to General-in-Chief Who Conquers the West and
Governor of Jīngzhōu 荊州."
Bólè's 伯樂 *Xiàng Mǎ Jīng* 相馬經 (Classic of Horse Judging) says:
"A horse with a white forehead extending into the mouth to the teeth
is called 'yú yàn' 榆鴈,
also called Dìlú 的盧.
If a servant rides it, they will die;
if the master rides it, he will be executed in the marketplace.
It is an ill-omened horse."
Someone advised him to sell it.
The *Yǔ Lín* 語林 (Forest of Discourse) says:
"Yīn Hào 殷浩 urged the Duke to sell the horse."
Yǔ 庾 said:
"If it is sold, there must be a buyer,
and it will again harm its master.
How can I be at peace with myself if I shift the harm to others?
Formerly, Sūn Shū'áo 孫叔敖 killed a two-headed snake for the sake of future generations;
this is a beautiful story from the past."
Jiǎ Yī's 賈誼 *Xīnshū* 新書 (New Writings) says:
"When Sūn Shū'áo 孫叔敖 was a child,
he went out on the road
and saw a two-headed snake.
He killed it and buried it.
Returning home, he saw his mother and wept.
She asked him the reason. He replied:
"A person who sees a two-headed snake is sure to die.
I went out and saw one, so it must be so."
His mother said, "Where is the snake now?"
He replied, "Fearing that others would see it later,
I killed and buried it."
His mother said, "He who possesses hidden virtue
will surely receive manifest reward.
You have nothing to worry about."
Later, he rose to prominence in the Chǔ dynasty court.
When he grew up, he became the Chancellor of Chǔ (楚令尹, Chǔ lìngyǐn).
Imitating this,
is it not insightful!"
When Ruan Guānglù (阮光祿) was in Shàn (剡),
he once had a fine carriage,
and he always lent it to whoever asked.
Someone was burying his mother
and wanted to borrow it but dared not ask.
Ruan (阮) later heard of this,
and sighed,
"If I have a carriage and people dare not borrow it,
what is the use of having a carriage?"
So he burned it.
The "Unofficial Biography of Ruan Guānglù (阮光祿別傳)" says:
"Yù (裕)'s style name was Sīkuàng (思曠).
He was from Wèishì (尉氏), Chénliú (陳留).
His grandfather was Lù (略),
the Minister of the Interior of Qí (齊國內史).
Fù Yǐ (父顗) was the Grand Administrator of Rǔnán (汝南).
Yù (裕) was erudite, thoroughly understood principles, and was discerning.
He was promoted successively to Attendant Gentleman of the Palace.
Due to illness, he built a residence in the Yěshān (剡山) mountains of Kuàijī (會稽).
He was summoned to be a Golden Purple Grand Master of Palace,
but did not accept the position.
He died at the age of sixty-one."
Xiè Yì (謝奕) served as the Magistrate of Yě (剡).
The *Zhongxing Shu* (中興書) states:
"Xiè Yì (謝奕), courtesy name Wúyì (無奕), was from Yángxià (陽夏) in Chén Commandery (陳郡).
His grandfather was Héng (衡),
Junior Preceptor to the Heir Apparent.
His father was Póu (裒),
Minister of the Civil Office.
Yì (奕) was known for his ability to judge character from a young age.
He was summoned as an assistant to the Grand Commandant,
and Magistrate of Yě (剡),
and was successively promoted to Governor of Yu Province (豫州刺史)."
There was an old man who broke the law.
Xiè (謝) punished him with fine wine,
to the point of excessive drunkenness,
and still did not stop.
The Grand Tutor (referring to Xiè Ān 謝安) was seven or eight years old at the time,
wearing green cloth trousers.
Sitting next to his elder brother Xiè Wàn (謝萬),
he advised, saying:
"Brother! The old man is pitiful,
how can you do this?"
Yì then changed his expression and said:
"Do you want to let him go, boy?"
And so he released him.
Grand Tutor Xiè highly valued Lord Chǔ,
often saying:
"Although Chǔ Jìyě doesn't speak,
he embodies the spirit of the four seasons."
The "Wénzì Zhì" says:
"Xiè Ān's courtesy name was Ānshí,
he was Yì's younger brother.
His family was known for learning and conduct,
Ān was broad, pure, perceptive, and far-reaching,
gentle, refined, and smooth.
Huán Yí, upon seeing him at the age of four,
praised him, saying:
'This child's spirit is refined and penetrating,
he will certainly follow in the footsteps of Wáng Dōnghǎi.'
He excelled at running script calligraphy.
He was successively promoted to Grand Protector,
and Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was posthumously granted Grand Mentor."
The "Jìn Yángqiū" says:
"Chǔ Póu's courtesy name was Jìyě,
a native of Yángdí in Hénán.
His grandfather was Xī,
Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍, General Who Pacifies the East).
His father, Zhì (治),
was the Grand Administrator of Wǔchāng (武昌).
Póu (裒) was young and had a simple yet noble demeanor,
and was known for his quiet composure.
He was successively promoted to the positions of Inspector of Jiāng (江)
and Yǎn (兗) two provinces.
He was posthumously awarded the titles of Attendant Gentleman of the Palace (侍中) and
Grand Tutor (太傅)."
When Magistrate Liú (劉), was in the district,
he was seriously ill and near death.
He heard the drums and dancing for the shrine of a god outside the gate.
He said sternly,
"Do not allow superstitious sacrifices!"
The *Liú Yǐn Biézhuàn* (劉尹別傳, Unofficial Biography of Magistrate Liú) says:
"Tán (惔), style name Zhēncháng (真長),
was a native of Xiāo (蕭) in Pèiguó (沛國).
He was a descendant of the Hàn dynasty.
Zhēncháng (真長) had refined discernment.
Even though he lived in a humble lane in a simple dwelling,
he was serene.
He successively held the positions of Left Clerk of the Minister Over the Masses,
Attendant Gentleman of the Palace,
and Magistrate of Dānyáng (丹陽).
In governing, he emphasized stability, tranquility, and sincerity,
and worldly affairs could not move him."
Someone requested permission to kill an ox from a cart to sacrifice to the gods.
Zhēncháng (真長) replied,
"My prayers have been made for a long time,
do not trouble yourselves again."
The *Lúnyǔ* (論語, Analects) of Bāo (包) says:
"Dǎo (禱, prayer),
means qǐng (請, to request)."
